messages.subject: Including an extinct area
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick, and BGBers

I am wondering if it is possible to include an area the no longer exists in the present day in a BGB analysis. (Sorry if this has already been discussed)

For example, I want to run an analysis to estimate the ancestral biogeography of some tropical fish groups that would have had an ancestral range in the Tethys region (Now Mediterranean/Western Indian Ocean/RedSea) which formed a centre of diversity in an open seaway that subsequently closed and broken down that region.

Would it be logical/possible for me to constrain some ancestral nodes to have a distribution in the Tethys, then in another time slice disallow the area and dispersal into it - essential coding the region as extinct for subsequent time slices.

If this is possible, I am assuming that in the tip ranges I would have the "extinct" region coded as all zeros. Would this be allowed, or would it cause an error in setting up the analysis?

I am attempting to do this at the moment so I will update on my progress or any errors I encounter.

Cheers

Pete

messages.subject: IBS2015 slides, and stochastic mapping
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently at the IBS2015 meeting in Bayreuth, Germany. It is great to see a lot of interest in BioGeoBEARS!

I just wanted to mention that I have put up some slides on my talk on Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping. It is in "Files", here:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears

2015-01-10_Matzke_IBS_stochastic_mapping_v3.pdf

I have worked a lot in the last week in trying to double-check all of the steps involved in stochastic mapping. It basically works and the event counts make sense, but the state/range probabilities that I get from averaging 1000 stochastic maps are not as close to the ancestral state probabilities from the maximum likelihood analysis as I had expected.  I've tried several variants and I'm still getting this result, so I am starting to wonder if

1. ancestral probabilities under ML model = downpass likelihoods x uppass likelihoods

and

2. average of many stochastic maps

...are not actually supposed to be identical. #2 is sampling linked histories with the ancestor->left, right cladogenetic events sampled jointly, conditional on sampled ancestors and the downpass likelihoods from above, and #1 is calculating the probabilities of each node and corner independently.

So, anyway, I want to be really sure about this before taking a stand one way or the other, so -- as I note on the wiki! -- stochastic mapping should be viewed as in development, i.e. in beta.

I'll post updates as I work on it more.

Cheers!
Nick

On Monday, 25 November 2013 21:48:44 UTC-5, Nick Matzke wrote:
> A question about large trees where the pie charts start
> overlapping:

>
>  > Attached is the DECj output ï¿½ with 97 samples the pie charts
>  > are hard to read, do you have a suggestion for how to spread
>  > out the output?
>
>
>
> So, that's a difficult question.  There's just not a ton of
> good ways to (clearly) display hundreds of pie charts on one
> page/screen.  A couple of suggestions:
>
> 1. You can increase/descrease the size of each pie chart by
> adjusting the "statecex" option in this command:
>
> plot_BioGeoBEARS_results(results_object, analysis_titletxt,
> addl_params=list("j"), plotwhat="pie", label.offset=0.45,
> tipcex=0.7, statecex=0.7, splitcex=0.6, titlecex=0.8,
> plotsplits=TRUE, cornercoords_loc=scriptdir,
> include_null_range=TRUE, tr=tr, tipranges=tipranges)
>
>
>
> 2. the example script plots the charts to PDF (everything
> between pdf() and dev.off()).  This enforces an 8.5x11 page
> size.  You could change the page size, or comment out the
> pdf() command and thus plot to the default R window, which
> you can resize with the mouse and then manually save to PDF
> or PNG.
>
>
>
> 3. You have access to the full range of phylogeny plotting
> options in the APE package, but this is not a specifically
> BioGeoBEARS thing.  E.g. one could imagine experimenting
> with circular phylogeny plots etc.  Most important question
> is, what is the end goal?  I view the pie charts as useful
> to the researcher to see just what the major trends are, and
> also what nodes are highly uncertain.  It may or may not be
> worthwhile to display pie charts for everything for a
> publication. Maybe piecharts for just certain nodes etc.?
>
>
> 4. One could also subset the tree and the results, again
> this isn't a BioGeoBEARS thing, it just takes R skillz...
>
>
>
> Cheers,
> Nick

2014-12-18 17:41 GMT+01:00 Nick Matzke <mat...@nimbios.org>:

> Answer about getting the probabilities of each state (each geographic range) at each node..
>
> Cheers!
> Nick
>
> ---------- Forwarded message ----------
> From: Nick Matzke <mat...@nimbios.org>
> Date: Wed, Dec 17, 2014 at 2:24 PM
> Subject: Re: BioGeoBEARS outputs
> To: Lukas Ruber <lukas...@nmbe.ch>
>
> Hi!  Thanks for the question.
>
> Yes, it's even easier than Lagrange to get the probabilities of each ancestral state. E.g. if the result object is "res", they are stored in the listed elements in "res":
>
> names(res)
>
> E.g. the probabilities of each states at each node are in:
>
> res$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node
>
> The probabilities of each state at each "corner" (branch bottom, representing the states instantaneously after cladogenesis splits) are in:
>
> res$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_bottom_below_node
>
> These tables have:
>
> rows: tips, then root node, then internal nodes -- numbered as in the APE package defaults or the prt() function
>
> columns: states (each state is a geographic range, e.g. for 2 areas there are 4 states/ranges: null, A, B, or AB
>
> See e.g.: http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#node_numbering
>
> Note that these are the state probabilities under the global ML model. Lagrange does state probabilities slightly differently, by fixing each ancestral state at each node and re-optimizing the model parameters under each constraint. They are typically similar but there can be some differences. See Matzke 2014, Sys Bio.
>
> Cheers!  Hope it works for you, let me know how it goes.
>
> Nick
>
> PS: Can I post this answer to the BioGeoBEARS google group?  It will help other people...
>

messages.subject: Dispersal multipliers and AIC
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nick,

I would like to test different dispersal models (dispersal multipliers) by setting different dispersal constraints to test for the directionality of faunal exchange.

Let's assume three areas (A, B, C)
In the first model I would like to allow exchange between all all areas
A B C
1 1 1
1 1 1
1 1 1

In the second model I would like to restrict dispersal from A to B to C
A B C
1 1 0
0 1 1
0 0 1

In the third model I would like to restrict dispersal from C to B to A
A B C
1 0 0
1 1 0
0 1 1

I only would like to look at the DEC model and want to compare the three resulting likelihoods with AIC. The DEC has 2 parameters. Is it correct that the dispersal restrictions do not manifest themselves in the number of parameters for the AIC? Hence for calculating the AIC = 2k -ln(L) I would use for all three models k=2?

Many thanks for your kind help.
Best wishes,
Lukas
